figures.caption: Figure 2. Pareto fronts of negative log-likelihood (∆NLL, red) and description length (∆DL, blue) relative to the best function identified, as a function of complexity, for each dataset. Lower is better. Points connected by lines show the best ESR functions at each complexity; isolated markers show the literature fitting functions. We show both the original form of the Bernardi function (Eq. 11) and our reparametrisation (Eq. 12). Complexity gaps are indicated by broken x-axes. The best DL functions clearly Pareto-dominate all literature fits besides the Bernardi function for the SMF, indicating a clear gain from using symbolic regression. Note that the Schechter results for the LF and SMF, and Press–Schechter results for the HMF, lie off the top of the plot. The HMF panel additionally shows the Pareto front of Press–Schechter-like (PS-like) functions (f(σ) ∝ 1/σ at large σ) at the two complexities where we find them.

Figure 4. Extrapolation behaviour of the top four ESR functions (solid coloured lines) and literature fits (dashed/dotted lines) for the LF (top), SMF (middle) and HMF (bottom). For the HMF, we show the top four ESR functions from the combined ranking across all 100 Quijote realisations (the data points and fitted parameter values are for realisation 50, but look similar for any realisation).

Figure 3. Comparison of the best ESR, Schechter and Bernardi fits to the LF (left) and SMF (right) data, for both the Sérsic (red) and cmodel (blue) photometries. The upper panels show the data and fits, the middle panels show the uncertainty-normalised residuals, and the lower panels show the per-bin ∆NLL contributions relative to the best ESR function which is therefore a flat line at 0 by construction (not shown). The errorbars on the upper panels show the asymmetric 68 per cent Poisson confidence interval (16th–84th percentiles) on the count in each bin, converted to log ϕ (these are typically very small). The middle panel uses the symmetric Gaussian approximation to the Poisson uncertainties: σlog ϕ = 1/(ln 10 √ N).
Figure 6. Top-five ranks of all functions appearing at least once in the top five of at least one of the 100 Quijote realisations.

Table 1. Top ESR functions for the luminosity function, ranked by description length (DL) for complexities up to 10. x ≡ L/109 L⊙. ∆DL and ∆NLL are relative to the rank-1 ESR function. The “Checks” column summarises the results of the physicality checks described in Sec. 3 (see notes below the table). Grayed-out rows indicate functions failing at least one check.

Figure 5. As Fig. 3 but for the HMF, comparing the top ESR function overall, and best PS-like function, to literature fits. Upper panel: f(σ) with data points. Middle panel: uncertainty-normalised residuals. Lower panel: per-bin ∆NLL relative to the rank-1 ESR function. Results are shown for Quijote realisation 50, but are similar across all realisations.

Table 3. Top ESR functions for the halo mass function, ranked by combined description length across all 100 Quijote realisations. ∆DL and ∆NLL are the combined values summed over all realisations, relative to the rank-1 function. Tinker and Warren are excluded from the ranking because their complexities are beyond the ESR search range. We also include separately the best PS-like functions. Parameter uncertainties show the 16th–84th percentile spread in maximum-likelihood parameter values across the 100 realisations. Grayed-out rows indicate functions failing at least one physicality check.
Table 2. As Table 1 but for the stellar mass function. x ≡ M⋆/109 M⊙.
